title: Zimmermann half-pi lace shawl
subtitle: A fingering-weight half-pi semicircle with a lace section and picot bind-off.
excerpt: A fingering-weight semicircular shawl using Elizabeth Zimmermann's half-pi construction, with plain garter in the inner sections and a 12-row leaf lace pattern introduced in the outermost section before a picot bind-off. Wingspan approximately 170 cm, centre-back depth approximately 65 cm. About 400 g of fingering yarn.
sourceNotes: The half-pi shawl construction is Elizabeth Zimmermann's invention, published in Knitting Without Tears (1971), §Shawls. The leaf lace panel in the final section uses a simple 12-stitch leaf repeat documented in Weldon's Practical Knitter, 3rd series (1887), §Lace Knitting. The picot bind-off is a standard technique with no single source.

knitting.gaugeText: 24 sts × 48 rows = 10 × 10 cm in garter stitch on 3.75 mm needles, blocked.
knitting.finishedSizeText: Wingspan approximately 170 cm. Centre-back depth approximately 65 cm. Blocked.

glossaryTerms.definition: Elizabeth Zimmermann's semicircular shawl formula: start with a small cast-on at the straight top edge and work increases on every other stitch on evenly spaced increase rows. Between increase rows, the number of plain rows follows a logarithmic sequence (3, 6, 9, 18, 27, ...) creating a flat semicircle without short rows.

A decorative bind-off that creates small loops along the edge: cast on 2 or 3 stitches, then immediately cast them off, working in a bind-off stitch at each picot. The loops form an even scalloped or spiked border.

content.text: A semicircular fingering shawl using Elizabeth Zimmermann's
half-pi construction
. Plain garter runs through sections 1 to 4; section 5 adds leaf lace, finished with a
picot bind-off
. Wingspan 170 cm, depth 65 cm.

The structure is the same logarithmic doubling schedule as the beginner garter half-pi, but in fingering weight with a lace layer added to the widest section. The lace repeat is 12 stitches wide and 12 rows tall; it fits naturally into the final section where the stitch count exceeds 300. Budget about 400 g (about 1,600 m / 1,750 yards) of fingering wool.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: About 400 g (1,600 m / 1,750 yards) of fingering-weight yarn

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 3.75 mm (UK 9 / US 5) circular needle, 100 cm or longer

items.name: Tapestry needle, scissors, blocking mat, pins

content.text: Gauge

24 stitches and 48 rows to 10 cm over garter stitch on 3.75 mm needles, blocked. The lace section may run 2 stitches per 10 cm wider than the garter sections, which helps compensate for the draw-in at the garter-to-lace transition. If your blocked gauge reads 26 stitches per 10 cm, the wingspan will be about 157 cm; add one more lace section repeat band to compensate.
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast on and sections 1 to 4

Cast on 9 stitches using the long-tail cast-on. Work the half-pi doubling schedule as for the garter version: 3 plain rows then increase row 1, 6 plain rows then increase row 2, 9 plain rows then increase row 3, 18 plain rows then increase row 4. All rows in sections 1 to 4 are plain garter. After increase row 4, stitch count is approximately 129 stitches.
Section 5: leaf lace
After increase row 4 (approximately 129 sts), work the leaf lace repeat for the 27 rows of section 5. Continue in lace through increase row 5, then for a further 36 rows to reach the full wingspan.
Leaf lace repeat (12 sts, RS rows): k2, k2tog, yo, k1, yo, ssk, k3, yo. WS rows: k all sts.
Repeat this 2-row unit for all RS rows in section 5 and beyond. The motif creates a slight diagonal leaf on each 12-stitch repeat.
Picot bind-off

Bind off as follows: *cast on 3 stitches using the cable cast-on method, then bind off 5 stitches; repeat from * to end. Each picot loop uses 3 cast-on stitches and 5 bind-off stitches. The picot loops sit as small points along the curved lower edge.
Stitch count check-ins
After increase row 4: approximately 129 stitches. This is the last garter doubling row; lace begins next.
After increase row 5: approximately 257 stitches. The lace pattern spans approximately 21 full 12-stitch repeats plus a partial repeat at each edge.
Common faults

Lace motif misaligned after increase row 5: the increase row added stitches that shift the 12-stitch repeat alignment. After any increase row, count the body stitches and re-set the first stitch of the repeat to the nearest 12-stitch boundary before resuming lace.
Picot bind-off too tight to block: the cable cast-on was worked at normal body tension. Work the cast-on stitches for each picot loosely, or use a needle one size larger for the bind-off row.
Blocking

Soak in cool water 15 minutes, press out in towels. Pin the straight top edge from end to end. Pin the curved lower edge to the full 170 cm wingspan, spreading each picot loop out to a distinct point. The leaf lace will open significantly with aggressive pinning.
Care
Hand wash in cool water, lay flat to dry. The picot edge retains its shape well after the first blocking.
What to try next
Add lace to section 4 as well as section 5 for a more uniformly lacework shawl. At the section 4 stitch count of approximately 65 stitches, a 6-stitch lace repeat is a comfortable scale.
